newsitem.title: GERMANY: German sick pay deal sparks hopes for end to dispute.
newsitem.headline: German sick pay deal sparks hopes for end to dispute.

text.p: Metal and engineering employers in the German state of Lower Saxony agreed Thursday not to enforce a law reducing sick pay, sparking hopes for a wider settlement that would avert threatened strikes in the sector.

Negotiators said that after 13 hours of talks in Hanover that they had agreed on a package maintaining sick pay at 100 percent of salary, overriding an unpopular new law allowing employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent.
"The accord is a breakthrough in the metal industry," Juergen Peters, chief negotiator for the IG Metall trade union said.
The law had been introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in October as part of austerity measures aimed at securing German entry to European economic and monetary union in 1999.

While Peters stressed that the deal was only applicable to the 90,000 metal and engineering workers in Lower Saxony, union officials said they were now more optimistic that similar agreements could be reached elsewhere in the industry.

An IG Metall official in the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia, where a similar attempt to end the dispute failed last week, said she was now optimistic that a deal could be reached before Christmas.
